title: The Backlash Against Polyester Has Gone Too Far
excerpt: Lately, the men of the internet who are obsessed with self-optimization have found a new fixation: their underwear
body: Lately, the men of the internet who are obsessed with self-optimization have found a new fixation: their underwear
Many standard pairs use polyester or spandex, or sometimes both

What are they doing to the environment and their bodies, wearing clothes that shed all of those microplastics and leach forever chemicals? They want the underwear of their ancestors—underwear made from natural fibers

On Reddit forums such as r/PlasticFreeLiving and r/SustainableFashion, people trade strategies for breaking up with polyester boxer briefs: “Any recs or leads to find linen cloth for making my own underwear?” one exasperated user wondered
Another wanted recommendations for all-natural underwear that would also be formfitting
He knew about organic cotton and hemp, he explained, but the problem was, they chafed
Seemingly everyone is interested in natural fibers
Whitney Crutchfield, who teaches textile development at the Fashion Institute of Technology, told me that she first noticed natural-fiber mania brewing among her sustainability-minded students
Then, a year or two ago, she sensed the discourse shifting to regular consumers
Across the internet, people are purging their closets of synthetics, swearing allegiance to only natural fibers from now on

The enthusiasm seems to cut across gender, culture, and politics. “I need my workout clothes to show my nasty sweat!” the fashion journalist Liana Satenstein wrote last year, praising the emergence of a new generation of natural-fiber workout wear amid posts about French pedicures and vintage Prada thongs. “Make all clothes natural fibers again,” posted Carnivore Aurelius, an anonymous wellness influencer who sells “beef collagen peptides.” Natural fibers are indeed pretty great
Silk, wool, hemp, linen, cotton, and the like—all of which come directly from either plants or animals—don’t carry the baggage of their artificial competitors
They’re generally understood to be biodegradable
And although the research is far from settled, synthetics have been linked to adverse hormonal effects
When I visited the website for a natural-underwear brand, a pop-up asked me what I looked for in my underwear: “Fertility health” and “supporting low T” were among the options
Natural fibers have also become an easy way to gauge the quality of a garment
Cotton, wool, and linen generally cost more than polyester and acrylic do, and they can look and feel luxurious in a way that many synthetics don’t
The reason finding a decent sweater these days is so hard is that so many of them are blended with synthetics, and one major reason for all of that blending is reduced production costs
Earlier this summer, when Gap released a reimagined version of a classic sweater from the early 2000s, fans revolted
What had originally been a chunky, cotton-blend knit turtleneck was now an entirely synthetic printed mesh
The anti-synthetic zeitgeist has transcended clothing; it is an attitude
Gen Z apparently now uses polyester as an insult meaning “cheap” and “inauthentic.” But the frenzy has gone too far

Are you really sure it’s always better to buy cotton or wool over a nylon blend? The whole point of man-made fibers is that they can have properties that specifically don’t exist in nature. “There are reasons that these things were produced in the first place,” Crutchfield said
When DuPont unveiled nylon—the world’s first synthetic fiber—to the public at the 1939 World’s Fair, it was a revelation

In the dawning era of synthetics, people would no longer be beholden to the limits of nature; instead, we had chemistry, which was going to free women from the drudgery of endless laundering and usher in an age of universal luxury
This did not, perhaps, play out exactly as one might have hoped, but even today, synthetic fabrics have plenty of benefits
Synthetics can enhance the performance of a garment, or the feel, or the durability, all of which contribute to a garment’s lifespan
The better it serves its intended purpose, the less likely you are to replace it with something new
A beautiful, all-natural raincoat isn’t an especially virtuous purchase if it doesn’t repel rain

On the whole, clothing with some percentage of made-made fiber requires less care than an item made with wool or silk or linen does—no hand-washing, no ironing, no reason to worry that moths might eat your favorite sweater
Sometimes, they really are the best materials for the job
The designer Issey Miyake’s famous pleated pieces are polyester because, as one textile expert explained to NPR, their thermoplastic qualities are what helps them keep their shape
Polyester actively repels moisture and dries quickly, which is why it’s used in so much athletic gear
Wool is stronger and more durable when it’s blended with a bit of nylon—not important for sweaters, crucial for hiking socks
A little spandex can help a pair of cotton leggings keep their shape

If we want the forgiving comforts of stretch denim and athleisure, “we have to make peace with the fact that synthetic fibers are going to be incorporated into our clothes,” Nancy Deihl, a fashion historian at NYU, told me
Yes, synthetic clothing can release microplastics—bad—but it isn’t clear how much swapping out your stretch pants does to meaningfully reduce your exposure
There is another problem with the natural-fiber obsession: Plenty of common fibers are neither synthetic nor natural

Semi-synthetics such as Tencel (the brand name for lyocell), modal, and rayon (otherwise known as bamboo) are made from natural plant material that’s been chemically dissolved and then reconstituted, a process that can be staggeringly toxic or ecologically responsible
Conventional cotton, for example, takes significantly more water to produce than lyocell and modal do

title: Trump Meant It Literally When He Said He Was Taking the Oil
excerpt: “We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Donald Trump said when he announced the capture of the Venezuelan dictator Nicol
body: “We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Donald Trump said when he announced the capture of the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro in January
Trump announced last week that he had made a deal with Venezuela to develop its oil reserves
Well, not so much a “deal” as a payment by Venezuela of tribute at gunpoint

In a social-media post , Trump announced that the oil “is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.” This is a surprisingly generous offer from a country that is much poorer than the United States and, like most countries, disinclined to hand over its wealth to foreigners as a present
Venezuela’s elected representatives did not approve this deal, because Venezuela’s representatives have not in fact been elected
The country also did not hold a referendum to approve it

Instead, after capturing Maduro, whom Trump had accurately denounced as a dictator, Trump installed one of Maduro’s cronies, Delcy Rodríguez, to govern in his place, in which capacity she has displayed roughly the same level of respect for democratic norms and civil society as her predecessor
Trump’s Venezuelan-oil heist has received far less attention than either his ballyhooed promise to avoid foreign wars or his ongoing quagmire in the Persian Gulf

Yet this operation reflects Trump’s foreign-policy instincts in their most nakedly amoral—which is to say, quintessential—form. [ Gisela Salim-Peyer: The hostile corporate takeover of an entire country ] The Trump administration laid the groundwork for its intervention by painting Maduro not only as a despot but also as the leader of a criminal syndicate
The Justice Department indicted Maduro and his allies for having “acted as leaders and managers of the Cartel de Los Soles,” a derisive nickname for the country’s kleptocratic rulers
Trump, however, apparently viewed regime change as a way to exploit this arrangement rather than transform it

His invasion followed the logic not of an American president promoting democracy or regional security, but of a mobster angry to discover that a small-time crook is running a racket in his territory without giving him a taste
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, The New York Times reported in July, “has become the de facto viceroy of Venezuela, holding sway over a sovereign nation in a way that no American official has since L

Paul Bremer III arrived in Baghdad in 2003 to run U.S.-occupied Iraq.” A salient difference is that Bremer’s occupation was intended to establish the grounds for free and fair elections, which did eventually take place
Trump, in stark contrast, casually told the Times in January that he expects the United States to run Venezuela for years
The new oil deal makes that outcome more necessary and therefore more likely
Rodríguez has tied herself to a policy that is toxic to both the left and the right sides of Venezuela’s political spectrum
Left-wing Chavismos despise foreign exploitation, and the opposition resents the Chavismos’ corruption

Exposing Rodríguez’s regime to free and fair elections creates a high risk of electing a government dedicated to unwinding Trump’s deal, which gives both her and Trump a strong motive to postpone such voting
When Trump deposed Maduro, some right-of-center analysts credited him with taking the first step in what they imagined would be a democratization project

The Wall Street Journal ’s editorial board celebrated the capture as “an act of hemispheric hygiene against a dictator who spread mayhem far and wide,” as did The Washington Post ’s ( headline : “Justice in Venezuela.”) Both editorials mixed praise for the operation with caveats that the important work of transitioning to a legitimate government lay ahead, while fretting that Trump was confusing the issue with loose talk about running the country and extracting its oil. “The president often shoots from his hip in these press conferences and would be wise to reconsider,” the Post proposed. “Mr

Trump also talked about ‘the oil’ far too much,” the Journal cautioned, adding, “Sooner rather than later, Venezuela needs another election.” [ Read: The bizarre partnership between the U.S. and Venezuela ] It all sounded a bit like congratulating Michael Corleone for taking a stand against organized crime by murdering the heads of the Five Families, while urging him to clarify his intent to focus the family business on selling olive oil at market price
Venezuela’s constitution expressly prohibits the sale of its untapped oil reserves to foreign interests
But Trump’s oil deal is designed to survive democratic scrutiny

Its “structure was deliberately intended to bind future Venezuelan governments to the agreement and make it difficult to unwind,” as The Wall Street Journal characterized the explanation given by a source involved in the deal
The Journal ’s reporting suggests that Trump’s Venezuelan partners may not hold the highest regard for legal niceties
Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan businessman who leads the private company partnering with the Trump administration, has been investigated for, though not charged with, money laundering

Diego Arria, a former Venezuelan ambassador now in exile in the U.S., told the Journal that the U.S. is working with Venezuelan government figures who are wanted in the U.S. for drug trafficking and other crimes
They are, in other words, Trump’s kind of partners

The president seems to despise democratically elected leaders (witness his current tantrum against Canada’s prime minister, or his yearslong feuding with South Korea, the European Union, and other erstwhile U.S. allies)

He has always gotten along swimmingly with criminals (since his early days engaging in social and business dealings with mobsters in New York) and dictators (such as Vladimir Putin, whom he simply cannot quit)
Trump’s favorite brand of partner combines disdain for the law and democratic norms with an absolute dependence on Trump
Trump has been saying for years that a vital objective in any foreign conflict is to seize the enemy’s oil
Indeed, he has been saying for years that he has been saying this for years. “I’ve been saying it for years
Take the oil,” he told The New York Times in 2016
Trump has shown time and again that his obsessions, even his most childish and comically sinister-sounding ones, are often quite earnest
In Venezuela, he is finally fulfilling a lifelong scheme.

title: The Absurdity of New York City’s Pied-à-Terre Tax
excerpt: New York City’s new pied-à-terre tax provokes strong opinions
body: New York City’s new pied-à-terre tax provokes strong opinions

Supporters argue that the nation’s first tax on luxury second homes will help balance the city’s budget and improve “a fundamentally unfair system” that “hurts working New Yorkers,” as Mayor Zohran Mamdani has put it
Opponents warn that the tax will alienate the rich people who power the city’s economy
Some homeowners fear that the new tax treats them as “ guilty until proven resident .” But Mamdani’s backers and detractors alike are missing the bigger picture
The new tax was created because the city has been spending more than it takes in
Neither has the dysfunctional property-tax system that made the tax so enticing in the first place
New York’s political class would do well to focus on solving these long-term financial challenges before they metastasize into a crisis
By spending political capital on a controversial but largely symbolic policy change, Mamdani has made that task even more difficult
For more than a decade , New York lawmakers had noodled around with creating a tax on pieds-à-terre, high-end residential units that don’t serve as year-round homes
A pied-à-terre tax, already used in London and Vancouver, was tossed around to fund city government and, later, to shore up the Metropolitan Transit Authority’s perennially strained finances
The idea gained new attention earlier this year as Mamdani stared down a significant budget gap
State lawmakers authorized the tax, which will apply to about 10,000 properties, to help city hall balance this year’s budget

Nonresident owners of condos and co-ops worth at least $1 million or houses worth at least $5 million will owe an extra tax in the neighborhood of 1 percent of their property’s market value. [ Annie Lowrey: Pied-à-temper-tantrum ] The new policy has triggered some overheated reactions. (Mamdani Derangement Syndrome is real.) One pundit described the mere act of listing the properties subject to the tax as “ a call to violence ,” even though local governments have let the public inspect the official list of property valuations and owners since colonial times
Other critics claim that the tax will cause wealthy New Yorkers to relocate

The revenue raised by the tax “is very little compared to to [ sic ] the TAXES PAID by the tens of thousands of people who are fleeing the City, never to return,” Donald Trump, a notable pied-à-terre owner, declared on Truth Social. “This dangerous political ‘experiment’ in New York will destroy what was once a great City and State.” In fact, the people subject to the tax can’t leave New York, because they are already, by definition, not residents
Still, these histrionic critiques are responding to a real shift in New York City politics
Bill de Blasio, for example—nobody’s idea of a fiscal conservative—sought to raise income taxes on the city’s highest earners in order to finance universal prekindergarten
Mayor Mamdani, in contrast, seems to view certain tax increases as virtuous unto themselves
His campaign slogan, “Tax the rich,” was a policy goal, not a mechanism
He unveiled the pied-à-terre-tax proposal with a video singling out the hedge-fund billionaire Ken Griffin and his Central Park South condo
Mamdani’s approach makes for good political theater

But the drama around the pied-à-terre tax, along with its turbulent implementation , has distracted from the underlying problem that made co-ops and condos so attractive in the first place: their inequitable tax treatment
Under state law, the property tax on these units isn’t based on their market value, but rather on the city’s estimate of the rent that a similar unit would fetch if it were an apartment
The result is that many are wildly undertaxed
A Bloomberg analysis of pre-COVID data found that the median sales price of a New York City condo was more than five times the city’s property-tax valuation
The journalists found an example of a Bronx home with an effective tax rate more than 200 times higher than one in Brooklyn

One of the more compelling examples of the disconnect between property values and property taxes was the condo that Mamdani cited in his video: The city considers Griffin’s unit, which sold for $238 million in 2019, to have a market value of just $15.5 million (and a taxable value, a separate city calculation, of less than $7 million)
The gulf between assessed and market value is just one issue
New York City, with the state’s blessing, has since the 1980s used gimmicks to shield homeowners (otherwise known as voters) from property-tax increases
But the benefits have flowed more to some properties than to others

By law, the share of tax paid by each of four classes of properties (essentially: single-family homes, apartment buildings, utilities, and commercial or industrial sites) can change only by a certain amount in a year
Over decades, the restriction has had the practical effect of preventing the property tax on homes in higher-demand neighborhoods from rising as quickly as their market value
That has left certain areas with significantly lower effective property-tax rates and smaller tax bills

One of the most regressive consequences of this system is the way it translates into higher gas and electric bills: The city has raised property taxes on utilities knowing they would pass the expense along to ratepayers
The pied-à-terre tax does nothing to address these issues

State and city officials could have put a dent in the city’s property-tax inequities, and even produced a windfall for the city, by simplifying the city tax system in a way that makes all property-tax bills more reflective of property values
That would mean allowing the share of tax coming from different types of property to shift with market conditions, and ending the different tax treatment of residences

None of this can, or should, happen overnight—the system was highly dysfunctional before Mamdani was even born—but the mayor has missed an opportunity to make a down payment on a generations-overdue reform
The pied-à-terre tax came into being only because the city faced a cash crunch and turned to onetime moves to deal with it (most notably postponing more than $2 billion a year in pension payments)
Unfortunately, it still faces one: The tax is expected to cover less than one-half of 1 percent of the city’s budget

title: Pied-à-Temper-Tantrum
excerpt: If you were trying to identify the spiciest policy affecting the fewest Americans, you’d struggle to do better than New York City’s pied-à-terre tax
body: If you were trying to identify the spiciest policy affecting the fewest Americans, you’d struggle to do better than New York City’s pied-à-terre tax
This spring, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Governor Kathy Hochul agreed on a plan to target extremely valuable homes

As of this fiscal year, homeowners will have to pay up to 6.5 percent tax on condos and co-ops assessed at more than $1 million; and up to 1.3 percent on multifamily houses assessed at more than $5 million
The out-of-town owners of a $10 million single-family home would pay $80,000 a year, on top of standard property taxes, for instance

Although the new fee is expected to hit only about 11,000 of the city’s 3.7 million housing units, it has dominated nightly newscasts and fronted tabloids ( PIED-A-TERROR, HOLD IT RIGHT TERRE! ) for weeks
A city-council hearing on the policy stretched for hours, with resident after resident complaining that it was confusing, unfair, invasive, confiscatory
New Yorkers have every right to criticize the rollout, which left a lot to be desired
Still, this controversy is a tempest in a walk-in closet
The pied-à-terre tax is a sound progressive option for a city with an excruciating housing shortage and obscene wealth inequality
More than that, it is a policy meant to make the city a city—populated by, enjoyed by, and built for people
Right now New York does not always feel that way

The brutal cost of housing has strained or wholly priced out many artists and care workers, retirees and young parents, blue-collar types and entrepreneurs. [ Ken Girardin: The Absurdity of New York City’s Pied-à-Terre Tax ] When wealthy families actually live in the units they own, they invest in the city in many ways
They buy bacon-egg-and-cheeses at the deli down the block
If they don’t live in their units, they pay property taxes without making extensive use of city services
Still, they contribute to rising housing prices without paying income taxes, spending at local businesses, or filling classrooms with children
They turn homes into safety-deposit boxes, “zombifying” their neighborhoods
No vacancies, no residents—it’s not a great scenario for a city as wonderful and in demand as New York
Local legislators have kicked around the idea of taxing pieds-à-terre for years
At first glance, the structure seems to hit apartments owned by members of the upper middle class harder than it hits brownstones owned by billionaires
In reality, the different rates are meant to equalize the burden

The city values houses by looking at comparable sales, yet state law prevents it from valuing apartments the same way; instead, buildings are appraised by estimating the amount of income they would generate if their units were rented out

The calculation tends to work out to a fraction of the actual market value, particularly for expensive units, hence the higher tax rate and lower threshold. (A condo that sold for $4 million would likely be assessed at about $800,000.) In two years, the city is expected to update its assessment system and apply a uniform set of rates
It’s confusing, and the complex tax has gotten a baffling rollout
The city’s Department of Finance published a roster of close to 1 million properties, along with their estimated market value and owner’s name
Anna Wintour, Cynthia Nixon, Deepak Chopra, Darren Aronofsky, and two city-council members were on the rolls

So were tens of thousands of middle-class homeowners, some of whom felt like Mamdani had personally doxxed them—even though property records were already public and city hall was legally obliged to publish the list
The DOF then sent 17,000 homeowners a letter asking them to prove that they were residents or to get ready to pay up

At the city-council hearing, an Upper East Side retiree described getting a notice saying that he might owe $52,000 on top of his current property-tax bill next year. “I filed an exemption,” he said. “The point is the government is assuming that I’m guilty unless I can prove myself to be innocent.” [ Annie Lowrey: How the richest people in America avoid paying taxes ] He has a point
To prove residency, the city is asking homeowners to furnish a federal or state tax return, a valid driver’s license, or a voter-identification card
These are records the government already has
Then again, filing for an exemption isn’t exactly hard
It certainly isn’t as hard as registering a kid for school, applying for food stamps, or purchasing a $5 million townhouse

And if city residents do not manage to get their paperwork done by the September exemption deadline, they will still be able to file an appeal with the tax commission at any point in the next six months
Concerns about the validity of the law have snuck through the turnstile along with concerns about the technicalities of the law
At the city-council hearing, a former union leader praised the politicians for asking the super-rich to pay their fair share
Still, he said, he worries about a friend who had purchased a townhouse four decades ago, and is now retired and living in the South
The friend “kept his brownstone here so that he can keep in touch with his kids and his grandkids,” he said. “It’s not only billionaires that are concerned
It’s the everyday, hardworking New Yorkers who’ve dedicated themselves to making this city work.” But, remember, the tax on brownstones applies exclusively to homes valued at more than $5 million

Is this friend really a hardworking New Yorker who had the good fortune to buy low? Or is he a millionaire who actually lives in Boca and thus might benefit from Florida’s homestead exemption? Such policies reduce or eliminate property taxes on primary residences, and may also protect them in bankruptcy proceedings

And they’re an analogue to New York’s pied-à-terre tax. (This specific kind of fee is sui generis in the United States, as far as I can tell, but popular, in both senses of the word, in foreign jurisdictions

title: Woodstock, Lilith Fair, and Taco Bell Rolled Into One
excerpt: Early Saturday afternoon at the Daisy Chain Fields festival, in Irvine, California, the 25-year-old singer Eli twirled in a tank top emblazoned with a cartoon g
body: Early Saturday afternoon at the Daisy Chain Fields festival, in Irvine, California, the 25-year-old singer Eli twirled in a tank top emblazoned with a cartoon guitar while singing songs whose plasticky violins recalled the kind of music played on the Disney Channel in 2004
Dancers waved poles with dresses attached to them as if they were flags

She took out her phone, whose case was shaped like a cute bear, and read some thoughts she’d jotted down. “This journal entry is to show you my fundamental belief that we must redistribute wealth,” she said. “We must love our neighbors no matter what they believe or don’t
We must unite with each other and radicalize

Eat the identity politics that deceive and divide us all, as well as”—here she broke into a ragged moan—“eating the rich!” Eli is a campy artist of questionable earnestness, but her statement was in line with the mood of Daisy Chain—a place where girlish aesthetics that are so often seen as frivolous could accompany calls for revolution

Organized by the 23-year-old pop star Olivia Rodrigo, the inaugural edition of the festival featured an all-female lineup and raised $20 million—half of which was donated by Melinda French Gates—for an array of women’s-rights organizations, including Planned Parenthood and the National Domestic Workers Alliance

Even as a brutal heat wave threatened to smother the energy, the fest felt like a cheerful coming-out party—an announcement of the political commitments of a generation of mainstream artists more famous for singing about the self than about society
Rodrigo patterned Daisy Chain off of Lilith Fair, the best-selling female-fronted touring festival that ran from 1997 to 1999, but the two events are a study in contrasts
Lilith’s co-founder Sarah McLachlan wanted to prove the viability of female musicians at a time when, she told the LA Times , radio programmers were reluctant to play two of them back-to-back

The lineup reflected a boom in singer-songwriters—Tracy Chapman, Jewel, Paula Cole, Indigo Girls—whose socially conscientious songs harkened back to the spirit of Woodstock (an obvious influence on the flower-powery Daisy Chain as well)
Lilith’s aesthetics were earthen and earnest—a celebration of an ideal of strong, serious womanhood, much to the perturbation of late-night comics who cracked jokes about Cole’s armpit hair
Today, women aren’t so marginal to the record industry; in fact, it can sometimes seem like Taylor Swift and her disciples are the record industry
But with power has come an inversion in content and style
The dominant female musical archetype of the 2020s isn’t the diva or the chanteuse—it’s the girlie , a term that conveys knowing immaturity and kitsch femininity

Girlies write songs about kinky sex while calling themselves princesses (as does the Daisy Chain singer Chappell Roan), or rap tough and fast while slathered in Barbie-pink body paint (as Doechii did on Saturday)
The word is gendered, but it refers to a disposition, and thus can encompass gay guys and even those shy and sweet straight men known as babygirls
Irvine’s Great Park was turned into a Lewis Carroll wonderland pocked with floral arrangements that seemed like crayon drawings come to life

Young kids ran around in tiaras while adults blended frilliness and adolescent-alternative stylings: blond locks with streaks of slime green, or the undying rebel-girl look of baby-doll dresses and Doc Martens

I wondered whether the commitment to daintiness explained even the dearth of shade at the fest; the tasseled umbrellas dotting the grounds were totally adorable and terribly unmatched to an El Niño August
Girlie nation has arisen slowly, over decades

As my colleague Sophie Gilbert reported in her book Girl on Girl , Lilith Fair’s vision of female artistry was sidelined as record labels and radio stations began to favor smiling, pliable teenagers such as Britney Spears
Twenty-first-century youths grew up with former Mouseketeers serving as aspirational figures—and, eventually, as cautionary tales about giving up one’s agency for fame
Following in the example of Swift, who built on her teen-princess image with her own formidable songwriting, the new female guard arose

Some, like Rodrigo and Sabrina Carpenter, were trained by Disney; others, like Billie Eilish and Rachel Chinouriri (an ascendant U.K. singer and a Daisy Chain booking), got their start at home, posting music online
All of them project control with every slickly witty, emotionally frank, personally revealing hit they write
What they haven’t projected much of, in their songs, at least, is the political edge of the Lilith crowd
Jewel broke out with an album whose title song made a shockingly frontal attack on bigotry (“You say he’s a faggot; does he make you sick to your stomach?”)
But today’s young stars mostly just side-eye society’s problems in lyrical tales of hookups, breakups, and anxiety
When Roan calls for a “Femininomenon” (one song title), she’s implicitly calling for feminist change, but she’s explicitly calling just for more girls to ditch their dudes
It’s not that Gen Z has nothing to say—many of these singers will readily riff about ICE and Gaza on their Instagram and in public comments
Rodrigo even delivered an onstage F.U. to the Supreme Court after the fall of national abortion rights, in 2022
But when it comes to their music, they prefer to focus mostly on the personal
Perhaps that’s because their milieu is the isolation and intimacy of the smartphone-enabled bedroom, not the social jungle of rock clubs and coffee shops

Maybe it’s because they watched progressive pop of the mid-2010s cheer Hillary Clinton’s failed presidential campaign and then spin itself into an even more didactic fervor during Donald Trump’s first term
On some level, girliehood may be a defensive posture amid conservative cultural backlash: a way to speak and shout and command lots of influence without being seen as threatening
Indeed, Daisy Chain inevitably raised the question of how potent mere cultural visibility can be

Lines of people snaked through the grounds throughout the day—some for art installations by female artists, and many for immersive brand activations, including a pink, larger-than-life Taco Bell Baja Blast that had been scrawled on with diary-cursive font
The festival was a co-production of the convicted monopoly Live Nation and felt, in execution, like a re-skinned version of moneymaking glitz fests such as Coachella
Eli’s rallying cry with a side of giggles aside, the fest was not destabilizing power structures—it was part of them
Rodrigo is probably not the person to figure out what true counterculture might mean in this, the most consumerist decade of human history

title: What Howard Zinn Got Wrong
excerpt: “What would Howard say?” This question, which Dave Zirin reports being “asked repeatedly” while he was working on his new biography of Howard Zinn , underscores
body: “What would Howard say?” This question, which Dave Zirin reports being “asked repeatedly” while he was working on his new biography of Howard Zinn , underscores how unusual a figure his subject cut in contemporary American life
Most historians live and die in relative obscurity
But 16 years after Zinn’s death, many people still look to him, not just as a scholar but as a kind of sage
Zinn first became famous—and, in some circles, infamous—after the 1980 publication of his best-selling work A People’s History of the United States
The book advanced an ambitious and unrepentantly radical reimagining of the nation’s past

Zinn rejected the conventional organization of history around “the point of view of governments, conquerors, diplomats, leaders” and declared, “I prefer to try to tell the story of the discovery of America from the viewpoint of the Arawaks, of the Constitution from the standpoint of the slaves, of Andrew Jackson as seen by the Cherokees.” What emerged was a new grand narrative, one that promised to reveal what mainstream history had long concealed and to offer a new moral framework for the past
In Zinn’s telling, the powerful were almost always up to no good, and ordinary people were the heroes of the American story
They courageously built movements for justice and sometimes even won, though it never took long for the oppressors to regroup
Unlike most best sellers, A People’s History never stopped selling
Each year during its first three decades in print, it sold more copies than the last
The book’s fans applauded its bottom-up, justice-minded approach to history, while its detractors dismissed it as a leftist morality play masquerading as a story about the past
No one could doubt that it changed the conversation about American history, not to mention the trajectory of Zinn’s life
By the time he died in 2010, he was an archvillain for the right and a secular saint for the left

Zirin’s fast-paced biography, The People’s Historian , is an answer to the most interesting version of “What would Howard say?” One hardly needs to squint to imagine what Zinn would have thought of the current regime in Washington, and readers curious only about that can put this book down after page 4, where Zirin declares, “Fascist movements taking orders from billionaire insurrectionists were the kinds of struggles that Howard Zinn demonstrated a willingness to fight and, if necessary, die to oppose.” But Zirin himself is after something more
He knew Zinn personally and collaborated with him on projects; he admires him deeply
Zirin believes we need more than Zinn’s opinions today; he argues that we need the deeper wisdom that emanates from his life and work
Zinn’s many gifts developed in the course of what was, by any estimation, a remarkable journey
He was born in 1922 to working-class Jewish immigrants in Brooklyn
In his early 20s he rushed to enlist in the fight against fascism, serving in the Air Forces during World War II

He would long regret his short tenure as a bombardier who dropped artillery shells on behalf of a compromised colonial power—as he would later come to see the United States—from such heights that he could not be sure where exactly they landed
Zinn’s willingness to admit he was gravely wrong is part of what Zirin loves about him

The people’s historian was a radical, but he was also a “happy warrior” who believed that people could change, and so could societies. [ Read: The new history wars ] As a participant in the civil-rights and anti-war movements, Zinn witnessed such transformations firsthand
He organized alongside his students at Spelman College as well as with famous activists, including Ella Baker and Daniel Berrigan
Together, in the 1960s and ’70s, they fought to change a country whose past and present were steeped in violence and white supremacy
The going was never easy, because, as Zirin tells it—very much in Zinnian fashion—they bumped up against so many villains in power
Sometimes it was the director of the FBI; other times, a reactionary university administrator
Any given campaign might be stymied, but the march went on
However dreary the news, the hope persisted for a better day
Zirin argues convincingly that Zinn’s life story vindicates one of his deepest convictions: that ordinary people and “small acts” can change the world
Zinn was right about this, and Zirin concludes the book with a quote from him that draws out the optimistic implications of his faith in bottom-up movements: “We have been surprised before in history
Indeed, we can do the surprising.” This is a compelling message for the current moment—and any other

Yet one can agree with Zinn on the power of the people to make change and still wonder whether recent history has revealed the limits of his wisdom. “Was he wrong to have faith in the people?” Zirin relates that some of Zinn’s devotees—“those politically raised on his ideas”—have asked him this question, in addition to the one about what he might say in any given situation
Zirin takes up the second query but answers it far less satisfactorily than the first

He acknowledges that “in 2024, 77 million voters checked the box for an authoritarian to take power once again,” and moreover that Trump “won masses of white working-class people and, according to political pundits, a not-insignificant number of Black and Latino men.” But Zirin does not wrestle with the meaning of these developments

Rather, he waves them away with invocations of the “tech oligarchs” and “autocrats” who are driving “our global descent into authoritarianism.” This is an homage in a way, a vintage Zinn move—evading tough questions about who “the people” are and what they really want
A People’s History of the United States appeared the same year Ronald Reagan was first elected president
In later editions of the book, Zinn would cast Reagan—like Jimmy Carter before him and George H
Bush after—as a creature of “the Establishment,” elected by a majority of voters but by a minority of the voting population and, hence, hardly the people’s choice

Zinn wrote something similar in 2003 amid the travails of the early War on Terror: “I wake up in the morning, read the newspaper, and feel that we are an occupied country, that some alien group has taken over.” The following year, of course, George W
Bush won the popular vote. [ Read: What if our ancestors didn’t feel anything like we do? ] Zinn was hardly the only academic to be thrown by this turn of events

title: How AI plotted an interstellar journey to Alpha Centauri
excerpt: An AI found a route humans couldn't: After a year of dead ends, the Fermi Explorer Mission handed its interstellar navigation problem to an AI system calle
body: An AI found a route humans couldn't: After a year of dead ends, the Fermi Explorer Mission handed its interstellar navigation problem to an AI system called Get Physics Done
In three days, it produced a novel trajectory combining known orbital maneuvers

The trick is flying close to the sun: The AI's solution has the spacecraft swinging closer to the sun than Mercury, firing its engine at each pass where solar power is four times stronger and thrust buys more energy
That keeps the solar panels—and the spacecraft—small and light enough for a $15 million budget
This spacecraft may never "win," and that's fine: The team openly admits that a faster spacecraft launched centuries from now could still beat theirs to Alpha Centauri by millennia
The point isn't to arrive first—it's to help answer one of the oldest puzzles in physics

The Fermi paradox cuts close to home: If intelligent life is common but keeps disappearing before it can spread, the Fermi mission's launch could mark humanity as the rare exception—or a cautionary data point. "Maybe in the next 50 years," says cofounder Philip Johnston, "there's some great filter that we do not pass through

That all intelligent civilizations, for some reason, do not pass through." " data-chronoton-post-id="1143247" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> A nonprofit organization called the Fermi Explorer Mission announced today that it intends to launch a spacecraft to our nearest star system by the end of 2029.  It’s a hugely ambitious mission—if all goes well, the spacecraft could take up to 80,000 years to arrive at Alpha Centauri, which is 4.4 light-years away
And the spacecraft will follow a novel trajectory discovered by an AI system developed by Physical Superintelligence (PSI), an AI physics research lab
PSI is launching today with $58 million in funding led by Breakthrough Energy, a climate-focused investment group founded by Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates
It’s not the first time this has been tried
In 2016, the billionaire tech investor Yuri Milner announced an interstellar mission called Breakthrough Starshot to launch humanity’s first spacecraft to Alpha Centauri
The plan was to use powerful lasers that would propel tiny probes to a fifth of the speed of light—fast enough to reach Alpha Centauri within 20 years
Milner pledged $100 million toward a proof of concept

But a decade later, nothing has launched. “We didn’t want to do another Breakthrough Starshot,” says Philip Johnston, the cofounder and president of the Fermi Explorer Mission. “We’re dead set on something actually launching.” The new mission, currently funded by individual private donors, is expected to cost just $15 million

To stick to that budget, “we are not constraining ourselves to doing it in a human lifetime,” says Johnston. “Let’s just figure out the way to get to another star.” The spacecraft will carry cargo weighing at least one kilogram

That will include artistic and scientific payloads, messages, and a copy of the Golden Record, a gold-plated disc of Earth’s sounds and images that NASA attached to its two Voyager probes in 1977 as a message to any civilization that might find them
Engineering an interstellar journey is extremely difficult
Alpha Centauri is about 25 trillion miles away from Earth
One of the fastest objects that humans have ever launched, the Voyager 1 probe, has been flying since 1977 and has covered less than 1% percent of that distance
At its speed, the trip would take more than 70,000 years
Johnston and his team spent a year trying, and failing, to find a way for a small, solar-powered spacecraft costing only $15 million to reach Alpha Centauri
They kept running into the knotty problem of how to give the spacecraft enough power without making it too heavy (and thus more fuel-guzzling)
After the Fermi team struggled to find a workable route, Johnston mentioned the problem in a podcast hosted by Alex Wissner-Gross, a physicist who cofounded PSI
Wissner-Gross offered to run it through an AI system the lab developed, called Get Physics Done
It’s open-source software that takes a physics research question, breaks it into smaller tasks, and decides which simulations to run, using AI models including Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s GPT
A week later, the AI system turned up a novel trajectory, to Johnston’s surprise
It combined well-known orbital maneuvers in a way the Fermi team had not considered, according to a paper that has not been peer-reviewed
It suggested that the spacecraft could first slow down so its orbit swings in close to the sun—closer than Mercury
On each close pass, it would fire its engine so that the solar panels get four times the light, and a burst of thrust delivered at high speed would buy more energy than the same burst anywhere else
Because the engine would run only near the sun, the solar panels could stay small and the spacecraft light
The system conducted the research mostly on its own for three days, running on a billion tokens, says Matt Pines, the cofounder and CEO of PSI

An astrophysicist on PSI’s staff steered it to follow the mission’s requirements, asked for a cost analysis and clearer charts, and checked the output for errors. “The fact that it came up with an entirely different mission profile, one that was creative and not one [the Fermi team] had considered—that was the more surprising aspect,” says Pines
Still, the model lacks a human researcher’s judgment and taste, he says

It has no reliable sense of which problems are interesting or which approaches are worth pursuing, so it often gets stuck chasing dead ends or failing to explore different approaches. “I don’t think we’ve yet figured out how these models can internally represent something like that,” he says of research judgment
Even if the Fermi probe launches, “we’re pretty confident that we will not be the first to arrive” at Alpha Centauri, says Johnston, since he expects spacecraft technology to improve
If an engine a thousand years from now is even 20% faster than today’s, a spacecraft launched then would still beat Fermi’s probe to Alpha Centauri by more than 10,000 years
But the Fermi project isn’t just an interstellar mission driven by engineering ambition
It’s also a quest to answer one of the oldest open questions in physics
In 1950, the physicist Enrico Fermi posed a puzzle: The galaxy has hundreds of billions of stars, most of them far older than our sun

title: Making the AI-powered case for legacy modernization
excerpt: For years, legacy technology has been a problem companies knew they needed to solve, but one they often struggled to tackle
body: For years, legacy technology has been a problem companies knew they needed to solve, but one they often struggled to tackle
The cost, complexity, and risk of replacing business-critical systems could make modernization feel like a disruption to manage instead of an opportunity to pursue
But with the rise in customer expectations and the changes AI brought to the economics of software development, that calculation is changing
Bupa’s modernization of its My Bupa mobile application offers a case study in what becomes possible when a legacy migration is treated as a business transformation rather than a technology rewrite

Bupa CIO of health insurance Asifa Sherazi describes the risks of waiting for legacy systems to become an emergency: “The end-of-life technology is a risk that compounds quietly, and then arrives all at once.” For Bupa, moving its application from Xamarin to native Swift and Kotlin improved the app rating from 3.7 to 4.7, while the user-perceived crash rate fell by nearly 24 percentage points on Android and eight points on iOS. “What they’ll notice is that when they need us, often at a stressful moment, it just simply works,” Sherazi says

Sanjeev Tripathi, senior vice president and region head of BFSI, healthcare, and public sector for Australia, New Zealand, and Southeast Asia at Infosys, contends that AI is helping change the equation. “The emergence of AI is fundamentally shifting the economics of modernization,” he says, reducing the effort, risk, and time traditionally associated with these programs
At Bupa, combining AI-assisted reverse engineering with forward engineering helped deliver the transformation in approximately 60% less time than would have been possible in the pre-AI era

Sherazi and Tripathi also highlight the human dimension of modernization: preserving institutional knowledge, giving teams capacity to adapt, and creating an environment where employees can surface problems early
Looking ahead, both experts see modernized platforms as foundations for more personalized, predictive and AI-driven experiences

The payoff of modernization may be less about replacing aging technology and more about building the flexibility needed for whatever comes next.  “Modern platforms will become the base for far more intelligent AI-driven ecosystems, where AI is not just an add-on, but it is built into everything from design to operations
That’s how the modern platforms will evolve, and the customer experiences will become far more personalized and predictive,” says Tripathi

For Sherazi, that shift is already changing the questions organizations can ask: “It used to be, can our platform support that? Now, it’s: is that the right thing to do for our customers?” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys

Full Transcript: Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace

Companies across industries continue to struggle to bring AI modernization to legacy technology stacks, increasing the risk of losing vendor support, degraded customer experience, and limited capacity for innovation
Two words for you: future-ready foundation

My guests are Asifa Sherazi, who is CIO of health insurance at Bupa, and Sanjeev Tripathi, who is senior vice president, region head of BFSI, healthcare, and public sector for Australia, New Zealand, and Southeast Asia at Infosys
This podcast is produced in association with Infosys
Megan: Thank you both so much for being here
Asifa, if I could start with you just to set the context for our conversation
There are seven million healthcare customers across the Asia-Pacific
Could you tell us a bit more about Bupa and the challenges it’s faced in its modernization plan? Asifa: Yes, absolutely
Let me start with something about Bupa that shapes everything we do
Think hospitals, clinics, dental, age care, digital health, alongside our insurance business
We reinvest back into the organization, so into our services, our capability, our teams, and our outcomes that we deliver for our customers
In Asia-Pacific, we serve around, as you said, seven million customers across health insurance and health services, individuals, families, corporate clients, patients
Our purpose, helping people live longer, healthier, happier lives is more than just a statement
It actually shapes our strategy, guides our investment decisions, and influences the choices our teams make every day
Now, for most of our health insurance members, the day-to-day digital relationship with Bupa begins through My Bupa, our self-service platform
It’s the front door for managing cover, updating policy details, submitting claims, checking entitlements
Alongside of it, Blua plays a complimentary role
Where My Bupa helps members manage their cover, Blua helps them manage their health, digital healthcare services, clinical support, preventative health
And together, they let us move beyond transactional interactions towards more personalized, proactive care
Our mobile app, My Bupa, was built on Xamarin, and Microsoft support for it ended sometime in 2024
We had extended support in place, so our customers remained protected throughout, but we were clear-eyed that this was a bridge, not a destination
The runway was finite, and it was shortening for us

We made the decision to modernize from a position of stability proactively for the long-term safety and experiences of our customer rather than waiting until circumstances forced our hand, because the platform carrying our most important customer relationship was in effect standing still while the world around it was moving
So you decided to act really proactively in that sense
And so, Asifa, what are some of the risks then of sticking with end-of-life technologies, and how will moving away from legacy technologies help you improve the customer experience? Asifa: Yeah
Look, the end-of-life technology is a risk that compounds quietly, and then arrives all at once
Once a technology is out of vendor support, the flow of security updates and fixes changes fundamentally

title: How engineered microbes could help feed the world’s crops
excerpt: Reinventing fertilizer with microbes: Synthetic fertilizer production accounts for roughly 2% of global greenhouse-gas emissions
body: Reinventing fertilizer with microbes: Synthetic fertilizer production accounts for roughly 2% of global greenhouse-gas emissions
Startups like Switch Bioworks and Pivot Bio are engineering soil microbes to fix nitrogen, potentially replacing a significant share of chemical fertilizers
The tricky biology of nitrogen fixation: Nitrogen fixation is energetically costly for microbes
Switch Bioworks is developing a genetic "switch" that lets microbes establish healthy colonies first and then triggers ammonia production when soil nitrogen drops low enough
Real fields, real stakes: Switch is currently trialing its microbes across six US states, with early results looking promising
Still, independent field trials remain critical, since company-reported data and independent findings can diverge sharply
A meaningful solution, but not a silver bullet: Even optimistic modeling suggests microbes can replace only about 50% of synthetic fertilizer at most

Synthetic fertilizer isn't going anywhere soon, meaning other emissions-reduction strategies remain essential. " data-chronoton-post-id="1143195" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Fertilizer is crucial for the global food supply, but making it uses a lot of energy and produces a lot of emissions
A growing body of research shows that seeding the soil around a crop’s roots with beneficial microbes can help feed the plant, providing crucial nitrogen to help it grow
This could help reduce the need for chemical fertilizer, production of which accounts for roughly 2% of global greenhouse-gas emissions

It could also cut costs for farmers, a big boon—especially as the Iran war has sent energy and fertilizer prices skyrocketing in recent months.  Humans have used biological fertilizers like manure for thousands of years, and companies have long been developing microbial fertilizers, including some that rely on genetic engineering

But it’s difficult to engineer microbes that can reliably provide nitrogen for crops while also thriving themselves.  A startup called Switch Bioworks is taking a new approach that essentially allows microbes to establish themselves and grow into healthy colonies before shifting into nitrogen-producing mode. “We have to reinvent fertilizer,”  says Tim Schnabel, the company’s founder and CEO
The air is nearly 80% nitrogen, but plants can’t use that “free” nitrogen directly because it doesn’t react readily with other elements
Instead, they rely on so-called fixed nitrogen, which has been converted into more reactive compounds such as ammonia
In nature, microbes can perform this nitrogen fixation
Some plants, like legumes, even have symbiotic relationships with nitrogen-fixing bacteria, housing them in nodules in their roots
Synthetic fertilizer is essentially industrial nitrogen fixation via the Haber-Bosch process , which uses natural gas to make ammonia that’s applied to fields
Biological fertilizers aim to replace some of the synthetic fertilizer with microbes that can help fix nitrogen for plants
But one challenge microbial fertilizer companies have run into is that it’s energetically expensive for microbes to make and release ammonia
Putting all their energy into nitrogen fixation can hamper their growth
There’s a certain level of colonization you want to see around the roots, Schnabel explains

It’s too expensive and logistically challenging to put all those microbes on the plant, so you have to rely on a smaller number of microbes to grow and divide, establishing the population.   Tim Schnabel walks in a cornfield where Switch is engaged in early trials
COURTESY OF SWITCH BIOWORKS Switch Bioworks is betting that a genetic switch is the answer
A genetic switch is a section or sections of DNA that controls how genes are turned on and off
In this case it works by activating genes that help trigger ammonia production in and release from the cell
The company is working on several options for setting off this change in its microbes

The leading one is to have the microbes react to the nitrogen level in the soil: Once it drops to a certain level, they begin producing ammonia. “You have this inherent biological reality, where it’s really expensive for microbes to fix nitrogen,” says Dan Blaustein-Rejto, director of food and agriculture at the Breakthrough Institute
It takes a lot of energy, and if they do fix the nitrogen, they want to use it for themselves, to build proteins and survive, he says
Adding genetic switches could help microbes grow and thrive and then help fertilize crops
Switch is currently trialing its product in six US states, though it’s two to three years from a commercial product, Schnabel says
It’s initially focused on corn, the most-planted crop in the US, with over 90 million acres in 2026. “It’s too early to tell exactly how well this works in the field,” Schnabel says
The company plans to harvest the plants in late October or early November, but as of August, some corn plants treated with Switch microbes already looked visibly healthier than those that hadn’t
And it’s still developing the products that will eventually make it to the market, he says

Switch’s products could significantly help to clean up agriculture. “There’s a lot of potential for these companies and products to help farmers reduce emissions,” Blaustein-Rejto says. “This could be a really important solution for a quite hard-to-abate sector.” While lab results have been promising, field trials are a crucial step in proving a product, Blaustein-Rejto says: “This is one of the final steps before they can go to market and make strong claims to farmers.” Independent trials are important as well, he adds, since there can be a large gap between a company’s reported data and what independent researchers find
Pivot Bio is another company working to bring microbes to fields
Since it was founded in 2011, its products have been used on millions of acres of crops
The company now produces a range of products: Some versions can be added when seeds are planted, while others are applied to seeds before they’re even on a farm
The company also recently expanded beyond corn to make microbial fertilizers for cotton, wheat, and small grains including sorghum and barley
Pivot’s initial challenge was trying to get microbes to produce nitrogen, whether they sensed it in the soil or not

Now the company is working to figure out how to make fitter, more robust colonies no matter the environment, says Travis Frey, the company’s chief technology officer. “Growers right now are experiencing a double whammy from the farm economics point of view,” he says

title: Before the infinity nets, there was ‘The Pacific Ocean’ – what origin stories focusing on Yayoi Kusama’s mental illness miss about her art

Cheng/South China Morning Post via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Stories of Yayoi Kusama’s life often begin after she <a href="https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/magazine/yayoi-kusama-biography-timeline/">moved to New York City from Japan in 1958</a> and found near-overnight success with her abstract <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/26/arts/yayoi-kusama-dead.html">infinity net paintings</a>. These evolved into the <a href="https://hirshhorn.si.edu/kusama/infinity-rooms/">infinity rooms</a> and <a href="https://dma.org/art/exhibitions/return-infinity-yayoi-kusama">polka-dotted pumpkins</a> that became social media phenomena decades later and the focus of her legacy after her <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/26/1102916697/yayoi-kusama-high-priestess-of-polka-dots-has-died">death on Aug. 14, 2026</a>.</p>

<p>Yet, this timeline misses a crucial first step in how she became one of the art world’s most famous international superstars: A year earlier in 1957, before her move, she journeyed over the Pacific Ocean to show her work in the United States for the first time in a hopeful first step toward her dreams.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757330/original/file-20260901-50-mbz6y2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A dark expanse made of mirrors, multicolored circles of light filling the seemingly cavernous space" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757330/original/file-20260901-50-mbz6y2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757330/original/file-20260901-50-mbz6y2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757330/original/file-20260901-50-mbz6y2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757330/original/file-20260901-50-mbz6y2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757330/original/file-20260901-50-mbz6y2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=497&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757330/original/file-20260901-50-mbz6y2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=497&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757330/original/file-20260901-50-mbz6y2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=497&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">Yayoi Kusama is well known for her infinity rooms.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/an-installation-by-artist-yayoi-kusama-at-the-liverpool-news-photo/83140914">Jim Dyson/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As an <a href="https://dornsife.usc.edu/ahis/profile/audrey-storm/">art historian</a> who specializes in the exchanges between Asian and American modern art, I believe it is important to consider not only her life after she hit it big in the New York art scene, but also how she got there from Japan.</p>

<h2>Crossing the ocean</h2>

<p>Viewers familiar with Kusama’s flashy polka dots may be surprised to see her bright color schemes in a painting she named “<a href="https://www.sothebys.com/en/auctions/ecatalogue/2019/contemporary-art-evening-auction-n10069/lot.30.html">The Pacific Ocean</a>,” which looks more like fire than water. This 1958 painting shares a glimpse into her state of mind looking out an airplane window as she flew from Japan to her first American exhibition the year before.</p>

<p>At the time, she didn’t know that she would finally achieve her goal of making a permanent move the next year. Reflecting back on this uncertain era from her new home in New York City, she painted many works named after the Pacific, the transition space between Japan and the U.S.</p>



<p>The pulsing red patterns are ambiguous. Is it sunrise? Sunset? Or a purely imaginary view? The paint glows with potential energy like a forge where Kusama could remake herself. Before leaving for America, she <a href="https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/magazine/yayoi-kusama-biography-timeline/">burned most of her old art</a>, wanting to leave her old self behind. </p>

<p>Crossing the ocean became another transformative step toward an uncertain future. Like the water’s surface, the painting’s swirling waves and currents draw the viewer in without revealing what is underneath its shadowy depths.</p>

<h2>Painting infinity</h2>

<p>Kusama’s lifelong struggle with her mental health is the most well-known explanation for her quest to paint “infinity,” which she famously called “<a href="https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/magazine/self-obliteration-yayoi-kusama-art-life/">self-obliteration</a>.” She embraced the stories that fascinated people, including anecdotes about her childhood nightmares and hallucinations that compelled her to paint patterns into the real world so she could exorcise them from her mind. </p>

<p>However, early paintings such as “Pacific Ocean” reveal other sources of inspiration that have been overshadowed by her larger-than-life persona and psychiatric struggles. </p>

<p>An artist’s origin story can turn her into a myth, but “Pacific Ocean” is a window onto a quieter, human moment, before Kusama became a global icon. It reveals how her relationship to the concept of infinity was also shaped by <a href="https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/exhibitions/yayoi-kusama-1945-to-now/">feelings of anxiety and awe</a> in face of the enormous Pacific Ocean and her unclear future. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757282/original/file-20260901-50-jc9t0x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Silhouette of person standing in front of a framed painting that, from a distance, appear to be uneven swaths of grey" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757282/original/file-20260901-50-jc9t0x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757282/original/file-20260901-50-jc9t0x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757282/original/file-20260901-50-jc9t0x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757282/original/file-20260901-50-jc9t0x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757282/original/file-20260901-50-jc9t0x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757282/original/file-20260901-50-jc9t0x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757282/original/file-20260901-50-jc9t0x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Yayoi Kusama created several paintings titled ‘The Pacific Ocean.’</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/photographer-walks-past-the-pacific-ocean-by-yayoi-kusama-news-photo/2151324136">Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>By repeating patterns that stretch and dance across the painting, Kusama suggests that this rhythm and pattern can go on indefinitely beyond the edges of the canvas. Even though neither the human eye nor a single artwork can contain the vastness of the ocean, the painting can capture a snapshot for a moment. </p>

<p>In this case, creating multiple paintings of the Pacific Ocean helped Kusama reflect on experiences larger than any single painting can encapsulate.</p>

<h2>Reflecting on a life</h2>

<p><a href="https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262551533/yayoi-kusama/">Research on Kusama’s early life</a> illuminates her as a complex figure who was constantly searching for ways to make a name for herself. </p>

<p>In 1957, before leaving Japan, she was motivated by hopes and dreams, but also plagued with fears: How would she get a visa? How could she get a job to support herself? Her first trip was disappointing because it ended without either.</p>

<p>In these early years, before she achieved the global success and popular recognition she hoped for, she was just a young girl looking out the window on her first international flight, uncertain of where her future would take her.</p>
