<title>What to do if your vote is challenged: Practical advice for midterm elections</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756637/original/file-20260827-60-uedg3o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8192%2C5461&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Many states allow same-day registration at the polling site.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/empty-voting-booths-on-election-day-royalty-free-image/1401415073?phrase=midterm+elections">adamkaz/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As the <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/us-midterms-129216">2026 midterm elections</a> enter the final stretch, it’s important to know your rights in case your vote is challenged.  </p>

<p>The best way to ensure that your vote is counted is to advocate for yourself. I’m a an attorney and lecturer for the University of Southern California’s <a href="https://dornsife.usc.edu/profile/karen-figueroa-clewett/">undergraduate civil rights advocacy initiative</a>, Agents of Change. Here are several straightforward ways to ensure your vote is counted and two practical remedies for you to consider if your vote remains challenged. </p>

<p>A major part of ensuring that you are able to vote is doing the necessary preparation before you even get to the polling place. Read on to find out how and where to register, where and when you can cast your ballot, and what numbers to call for any information you can’t find online.</p>

<h2>Are you registered to vote? Check it out</h2>

<p>Before you vote, you need to ensure that you’re registered to vote. You can verify your registration status using this <a href="https://www.usvotefoundation.org/am-i-registered">tool</a>. If you can’t use an online tool, then call your local election office or a voter help line like the ones listed in the hotline section below.</p>

<p>If you find you’re not registered, you can use this <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/electronic-or-online-voter-registration.aspx#Table%20of%20states%20w/ovr">tool</a> from the National Conference of State Legislatures to find your state’s online registration application. If you need to do this in person, then call your local election office for instructions.</p>

<p>At this point, you may have missed your state’s deadline for voter registration. But it may not be too late to register.</p>

<p>Many states allow same-day registration at the polling site. You can find your state’s same-day voter laws detailed <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/same-day-registration.aspx">here</a>. Ask the poll worker, at the correct polling location, for a same-day registration form; complete the form and then ask for a “conditional ballot.” A conditional ballot allows election officials to count your vote after verifying your voter eligibility. If you can’t research online, you can call your local election office to find out if you can register on Election Day.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Three young men with backpacks, talking; one of them is reading something on a clipboard he's holding." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Marchellos Scott, right, helps Morehouse College students fill out a voter registration form at a college registration booth on Aug. 19, 2024, in Atlanta.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/marchellos-scott-helps-morehouse-college-students-fill-out-news-photo/2168355994?adppopup=true">Elijah Nouvelage/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Gather documents to verify your identity</h2>

<p>If you live in a state that requires identity verification to vote in person, gather the required documents – which may range from a driver’s license to bank statements with identifying information – before traveling to the correct polling place. You can find your county election office’s contact information <a href="https://www.usvotefoundation.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm">here</a>. This <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id.aspx">webpage</a> includes a table listing each state’s acceptable ID documents and possible exceptions for some people. You may also call your local election office to find out what’s required.</p>

<p>Absentee voters: Locate your state’s identity verification rules <a href="https://www.vote.org/voter-id-laws/">here</a>.</p>

<h2>Find the correct polling location</h2>

<p>You can ensure that you’re headed to the right polling place with this <a href="https://www.vote.org/polling-place-locator/">tool</a>. Or call your county election office to find your polling place and its hours of operation; you can look up your county’s election office contact information <a href="https://www.usvotefoundation.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm">here</a>. </p>

<p>Once you know your polling place and its hours, you can go there and check in. In most cases, you’ll be handed a ballot, shown where to vote and asked to put your ballot in a machine or a box, and then you can go merrily along your way. </p>

<p>But the moment of check-in is where things might go wrong. </p>

<h2>Problems at your polling place</h2>

<p>Here are potential vote challenges and ways to overcome them.  </p>

<p>Possibility No. 1: Out-of-order polling machines. </p>

<p>If you’re asked to leave because of malfunctioning machines, don’t. Instead, ask for a paper ballot. </p>

<p>Possibility No. 2: You’re in line and officials announce the polls have closed.</p>

<p>If you’re in line at the polling location before it closes, don’t let them turn you away at closing time if you haven’t voted. You have the legal right to vote under those circumstances, so <a href="https://www.vote.org/election-protection/">stay in line and wait to cast your ballot</a>.  </p>

<p>Possibility No. 3: You’re not on the registered voters list. </p>

<p>If you’re told you can’t vote because your name is not on the voter roster, <a href="https://www.aclu.org/know-your-rights/voting-rights#what-are-my-general-rights-on-election-day">ask the poll site worker to check again</a> and to check what’s called the list of supplemental voters. If they still can’t find your name, ask the poll worker to verify that you’re at the right location.  </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Three people sitting at computer screens at a table with a black tablecloth on it" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=8%2C8%2C5982%2C3979&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Poll workers want you to vote. But sometimes there are problems.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/poll-workers-wait-for-voters-during-early-voting-at-laurel-news-photo/1244293258?phrase=poll%20workers&amp;adppopup=true">Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Possibility No. 4: Someone claims you shouldn’t be allowed to vote.</p>

<p>If your voting eligibility remains challenged after ensuring you’re at the right polling location, <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/provisional-ballots.aspx">ask to cast a provisional ballot</a>, which is available in every state except Idaho and Minnesota. You can find details about your particular state’s provisional ballot rules <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/provisional-ballots.aspx">here</a>. </p>

<p>Track your provisional ballot <a href="https://www.vote.org/ballot-tracker-tools/">here</a>.</p>

<h2>Call a hotline</h2>

<p>If you are not given a provisional ballot, call an election hotline for help. Here are four hotlines, run by members of the nonpartisan <a href="https://866ourvote.org/about/">Election Protection coalition</a>, that can help you: </p>

<p>English: 866-OUR-VOTE/866-687-8683, the <a href="https://www.lawyerscommittee.org/project/election-protection/">Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law</a></p>

<p>Spanish: 888-VE-Y-VOTA/888-839-8682, the <a href="https://naleo.org/es/vota/">National Association of Latino Elected and Appointed Officials Education Fund</a></p>

<p>Asian Languages: 888-API-VOTE/888-274-8683, <a href="https://apiavote.org/how-to-vote/multilingual-voter-hotline/">Asian and Pacific Islander American Vote</a></p>

<p>Arabic: 844-YALLA-US/844-925-5287, <a href="https://www.aaiusa.org/yalla-vote">Arab American Institute</a></p>

<h2>Report voter intimidation</h2>

<p>If someone tries to scare you into voting or not voting for a candidate, stand your ground and demand a ballot from the poll site, call one of the hotlines above to report the intimidation, and file a claim with the FBI later by phone at 800-CALL-FBI – 800-225-5324 – or online at <a href="https://tips.fbi.gov">tips.fbi.gov</a>. </p>

<h2>File a lawsuit</h2>

<p>If you are still blocked from voting, consider legal action – but get advice on your exact situation from one of the hotlines, which have free lawyers on hand. It’s a good idea to write down the names of people who prevented you from voting and to ask people who witnessed the incident for their contact information.</p>

body: Many states allow same-day registration at the polling site. adamkaz/Getty Images As the 2026 midterm elections enter the final stretch, it’s important to know your rights in case your vote is challenged
The best way to ensure that your vote is counted is to advocate for yourself
I’m a an attorney and lecturer for the University of Southern California’s undergraduate civil rights advocacy initiative , Agents of Change
Here are several straightforward ways to ensure your vote is counted and two practical remedies for you to consider if your vote remains challenged
A major part of ensuring that you are able to vote is doing the necessary preparation before you even get to the polling place
Read on to find out how and where to register, where and when you can cast your ballot, and what numbers to call for any information you can’t find online
Are you registered to vote? Check it out Before you vote, you need to ensure that you’re registered to vote
You can verify your registration status using this tool
If you can’t use an online tool, then call your local election office or a voter help line like the ones listed in the hotline section below
If you find you’re not registered, you can use this tool from the National Conference of State Legislatures to find your state’s online registration application
If you need to do this in person, then call your local election office for instructions
At this point, you may have missed your state’s deadline for voter registration
Many states allow same-day registration at the polling site
You can find your state’s same-day voter laws detailed here

Ask the poll worker, at the correct polling location, for a same-day registration form; complete the form and then ask for a “conditional ballot.” A conditional ballot allows election officials to count your vote after verifying your voter eligibility
If you can’t research online, you can call your local election office to find out if you can register on Election Day
Marchellos Scott, right, helps Morehouse College students fill out a voter registration form at a college registration booth on Aug. 19, 2024, in Atlanta

Elijah Nouvelage/AFP via Getty Images Gather documents to verify your identity If you live in a state that requires identity verification to vote in person, gather the required documents – which may range from a driver’s license to bank statements with identifying information – before traveling to the correct polling place
You can find your county election office’s contact information here
This webpage includes a table listing each state’s acceptable ID documents and possible exceptions for some people
You may also call your local election office to find out what’s required
Absentee voters: Locate your state’s identity verification rules here
Find the correct polling location You can ensure that you’re headed to the right polling place with this tool
Or call your county election office to find your polling place and its hours of operation; you can look up your county’s election office contact information here
Once you know your polling place and its hours, you can go there and check in
In most cases, you’ll be handed a ballot, shown where to vote and asked to put your ballot in a machine or a box, and then you can go merrily along your way
But the moment of check-in is where things might go wrong
Problems at your polling place Here are potential vote challenges and ways to overcome them
Possibility No. 1: Out-of-order polling machines
If you’re asked to leave because of malfunctioning machines, don’t
Possibility No. 2: You’re in line and officials announce the polls have closed
If you’re in line at the polling location before it closes, don’t let them turn you away at closing time if you haven’t voted
You have the legal right to vote under those circumstances, so stay in line and wait to cast your ballot
Possibility No. 3: You’re not on the registered voters list
If you’re told you can’t vote because your name is not on the voter roster, ask the poll site worker to check again and to check what’s called the list of supplemental voters
If they still can’t find your name, ask the poll worker to verify that you’re at the right location
Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images Possibility No. 4: Someone claims you shouldn’t be allowed to vote
If your voting eligibility remains challenged after ensuring you’re at the right polling location, ask to cast a provisional ballot , which is available in every state except Idaho and Minnesota
You can find details about your particular state’s provisional ballot rules here
Call a hotline If you are not given a provisional ballot, call an election hotline for help

Scott Applewhite</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The fate of President Donald Trump’s <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/18/us/politics/trump-ballroom-construction.html">estimated US$400 million White House ballroom</a> may hinge on the little-known and somewhat surprising rules as to when the federal government and its agencies can accept privately donated funds.</p>

<p>That’s because Trump’s using the fact that he’s been <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/white-house/republicans-propose-1-billion-taxpayer-dollars-secure-trump-ballroom-rcna343637">accepting private donations</a> to <a href="https://apnews.com/article/donors-to-trump-white-house-ballroom-d4dd174eeb30ac244354a5a25551a86b">pay for at least some of the project’s cost</a> as a justification for not needing Congress’ explicit authorization.</p>

<p>While a <a href="https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/opinions/docs/2026/08/26-5123-2187096.pdf">federal appeals court on Aug. 7, 2026, disagreed</a> with the Trump administration, the Supreme Court on Aug. 31 said <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/26a203_2b8e.pdf">construction could go on</a>. The 5-4 majority found that the preservationists who brought the case lacked standing, or legal grounds, to bring it in the first place because they were not directly harmed by the ballroom project. The majority did not address the underlying legal issues, which may or may not be resolved at a later date.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://law.ucla.edu/faculty/faculty-profiles/ellen-p-aprill">scholar of nonprofit and tax-exempt law</a> who has studied for decades how the law governs deductible charitable contributions, <a href="https://repository.uclawsf.edu/hastings_law_journal/vol74/iss6/2/">including those to the government</a>, I find that this case calls for an explanation of the role that such private donations may play in any federal government project or activity. An intricate statutory dance is required for taxpayers to make donations to particular government agencies or for particular government purposes.</p>

<h2>Giving to the government</h2>

<p>You may not realize that you can make potentially tax-deductible contributions to the federal government itself. An official <a href="https://www.pay.gov/public/search/global?formSearchCategory=Donation+Contribution">website lists almost two dozen programs</a>, including the National Endowment for the Humanities, the National Arboretum and AmeriCorps, to which United States citizens can donate.</p>

<p>But such donations to government agencies are allowed only if Congress has granted the agency statutory authority to receive those funds. Moreover, authorized private donations are treated as if <a href="https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-06-382sp.pdf">they have been appropriated by Congress</a>.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://yalelawjournal.org/article/congress-power-of-the-purse">federal government has accepted donations</a> voluntarily made by Americans <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/339/87/">since its founding</a>.</p>

<p>What’s more, the <a href="https://fiscal.treasury.gov/about-us">Bureau of Fiscal Services</a> – the central bank account and financial manager for the federal government – <a href="https://fiscal.treasury.gov/financing/gifts-to-government">explains</a> that it “may accept gifts donated to the United States Government” and that the account for such gifts, which dates back to 1843, was established “to accept gifts, such as bequests, from individuals wishing to express their patriotism to the United States.” Such gifts, however, are subject to restrictions.</p>

<p>In this context, according to the reasoning of the majority in the appeals court case, that means spending donated funds to preserve the existing East Wing would have been automatically allowed because it <a href="https://www.nps.gov/whho/index.htm">stood on a national park</a>, and the National Park Service is an <a href="https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title54-section101101&amp;num=0&amp;edition=prelim">agency to which individuals can donate</a>; spending those funds to build something new to replace that structure would not be allowed unless Congress had authorized the project.</p>

<p>But the Trump administration has <a href="https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1192/vote_119_2_00139.htm">failed so far</a> to <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/20/ballroom-security-funding-reconciliation-00930193">obtain the needed congressional authorization</a> and appropriations for the ballroom. </p>

            </figcaption>

<h2>Statutory restrictions</h2>

<p>Since 1982, a provision of the United States Code, the official codification of all the nation’s general and permanent federal statutes, has required that these “patriotic” donations be devoted exclusively to <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/31/3113">reducing the national debt</a>.</p>

<p>By law, federal agencies cannot augment congressional appropriations. The <a href="https://repository.uclawsf.edu/hastings_law_journal/vol74/iss6/2/">Miscellaneous Receipts Act</a> requires that “an official or agent of the Government receiving money for the Government from any source shall deposit the money in the Treasury as soon as practicable without deduction for any charge or claim.”</p>

<p>Despite this seemingly absolute language, government agencies are permitted to accept gifts of money or other property when – and to the extent – they are <a href="https://www.gao.gov/assets/210/202819.pdf">given explicit statutory authority</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://uclaschooloflaw-my.sharepoint.com/personal/aprill_law_ucla_edu/Documents/Documents/Governmental%20Charitable%20Entities/22%20U.S.C.%20%C2%A7%202697(a)">Agencies with the authority to accept gifts</a> include the Justice Department, the State Department and the Library of Congress.</p>

<p>But any money, including donated funds, must be spent only as Congress directed in establishing the agency mission. The mission of the National Park Service is the conservation and preservation of the land and structures under its jurisdiction.</p>

<p>In contrast, the <a href="https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/get-involved/write-or-call/">White House does not</a> have this authority. Its own website states that it “is unable to accept cash, checks, bonds … or other monetary equivalents” as gifts from private citizens.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755256/original/file-20260820-50-8epbwu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Donald Trump speaks to people in a ballroom with gold-framed paintings." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755256/original/file-20260820-50-8epbwu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755256/original/file-20260820-50-8epbwu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755256/original/file-20260820-50-8epbwu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755256/original/file-20260820-50-8epbwu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755256/original/file-20260820-50-8epbwu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755256/original/file-20260820-50-8epbwu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755256/original/file-20260820-50-8epbwu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>‘No instance in American history’</h2>

<p>That’s in part why the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit held on Aug. 7 that <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-calls-white-house-ballroom-military-complex-supreme/story?id=135782053">Trump could not build the ballroom</a> on the site of the <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/the-east-wing-of-the-white-house-has-been-demolished-heres-a-look-at-its-history">former East Wing building</a>.</p>

<p>The two judges in the majority concluded that neither the National Park Service, which is the <a href="https://www.nps.gov/whho/index.htm">steward for the national park</a> on which the White House stands, nor Trump himself had satisfied all the statutory requirements needed to undertake building of the above-ground ballroom. It did not block work on an <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/17/nx-s1-5931758/trump-wants-to-build-an-expanded-bunker-under-the-white-house-a-historian-weighs-in">underground military bunker</a> the Trump administration began renovating after it <a href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-white-house-ballroom-57512e0d91432f75529946fddfbfe2c5">demolished the East Wing in October 2025</a>.</p>



<p>That some, most or even all the funding comes from private donations does not protect the administration’s right to proceed with <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2025/07/the-white-house-announces-white-house-ballroom-construction-to-begin/">construction of the 90,000-square-foot</a> (8,361-square-meter) ballroom because it has <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/20/ballroom-security-funding-reconciliation-00930193">failed so far to obtain congressional authorization</a> and appropriations for this project, the majority explained.</p>

<p><a href="https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title40-section8106&amp;num=0&amp;edition=prelim">Crucial to this conclusion was a statute</a> declaring, “A building or structure shall not be erected on any reservation, park, or public grounds of the Federal Government in the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress.”</p>

<p>“We are aware of no instance in American history in which a President unilaterally and using privately collected funds demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorized to be built and American taxpayers paid for,” the majority opinion says. “Until now.”</p>

<p>The four dissenting justices in the Aug. 31 Supreme Court decision seemed to agree that there is “<a href="https://www.wsj.com/us-news/law/supreme-court-allows-trump-to-keep-building-white-house-ballroom-d45a7c1c?mod=hp_lead_pos1">an apparent absence of statutory authority</a>” for the project, noting that Congress must expressly approve the construction of any “building or structure” on any federal park in the District of Columbia. </p>

<h2>Satisfying 2 statutes</h2>

<p>The Trump administration has pointed to two possible statutes it says provides the necessary authority to build the ballroom.</p>

<p><a href="https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title54-section100101&amp;num=0&amp;edition=prelim">One involves the purposes</a> for which the National Park Service can spend its funds, including privately donated funds. The <a href="https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:3%20section:105%20edition:prelim)">other grants the president the ability to spend funds</a> for, among other items, “the care, maintenance, repair, alteration, refurnishing, [and] improvement” of the executive residence at the White House – funds that “are authorized to be appropriated each fiscal year.”</p>

<p>The majority in the appeals court decision explained that authority for the president to construct the ballroom requires satisfying both of those statutes; neither alone suffices.</p>

<p>And it rejected the reliance on the National Park Service provision alone. That statute limits use of the service’s funds, in the words of the majority, to “the identified purposes of conservation and preservation.”</p>

<p>In particular, the majority ruled, the provision does not authorize the construction of a new building. Further, it held, the National Park Service provision cannot authorize the president to lead the project; only the provision related to the executive residence can do that.</p>

<p>As to the executive residence provision, the majority opinion explains that it “does not expressly grant the President any independent authority.”</p>

<p>Instead, the majority held, the president must rely on “an accompanying appropriation.” The court found no such accompanying appropriation.</p>

<p>The Supreme Court majority, in its decision, did not address the merits of the argument. So even as the case continues, the ruling means opponents of the ballroom project will need to find someone who’s suffered actual harm in order to overcome this hurdle.</p>

Crucial to this conclusion was a statute declaring, “A building or structure shall not be erected on any reservation, park, or public grounds of the Federal Government in the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress.” “We are aware of no instance in American history in which a President unilaterally and using privately collected funds demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorized to be built and American taxpayers paid for,” the majority opinion says. “Until now.” The four dissenting justices in the Aug. 31 Supreme Court decision seemed to agree that there is “ an apparent absence of statutory authority ” for the project, noting that Congress must expressly approve the construction of any “building or structure” on any federal park in the District of Columbia
Satisfying 2 statutes The Trump administration has pointed to two possible statutes it says provides the necessary authority to build the ballroom
One involves the purposes for which the National Park Service can spend its funds, including privately donated funds

The other grants the president the ability to spend funds for, among other items, “the care, maintenance, repair, alteration, refurnishing, [and] improvement” of the executive residence at the White House – funds that “are authorized to be appropriated each fiscal year.” The majority in the appeals court decision explained that authority for the president to construct the ballroom requires satisfying both of those statutes; neither alone suffices
And it rejected the reliance on the National Park Service provision alone

That statute limits use of the service’s funds, in the words of the majority, to “the identified purposes of conservation and preservation.” In particular, the majority ruled, the provision does not authorize the construction of a new building
Further, it held, the National Park Service provision cannot authorize the president to lead the project; only the provision related to the executive residence can do that

As to the executive residence provision, the majority opinion explains that it “does not expressly grant the President any independent authority.” Instead, the majority held, the president must rely on “an accompanying appropriation.” The court found no such accompanying appropriation
The Supreme Court majority, in its decision, did not address the merits of the argument

<title>How students at Colorado State helped teach their community to stop talking past each other and manage complex problems</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753755/original/file-20260812-50-33gzn2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5461%2C3640&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Moving past debates and two-minute comment periods can help communities work together.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/business-team-and-dialog-boxes-royalty-free-image/812513444?adppopup=true">ALotOfPerople/iStock via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>On a Thursday evening in Fort Collins, Colorado, community members gathered around tables to discuss whether the city should allow marijuana dispensaries within city limits. </p>

<p>Rather than take turns for two minutes at a microphone, the participants considered various viewpoints, engaged with quality information and focused on exploring solutions that worked to mitigate the concerns of the critics but still supported the goals of the advocates.</p>

<p>Gatherings like this one have happened more than 500 times in and around the northern Colorado town over the past 20 years. Each was facilitated by college students. While <a href="https://thehill.com/opinion/campaign/4131461-the-vicious-cycle-of-political-polarization/">outrage and polarization dominate many political discussions</a>, these events provide compelling evidence that when offered a more nuanced way of engaging, the public recognizes the value and calls for more. </p>

<p>I’m a <a href="https://scholar.google.it/citations?user=5Ly9Y6YAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">communication studies professor</a> with a background in argumentation and debate. I founded the Colorado State University Center for Public Deliberation in 2006 based on the theory that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/comt.12055">democracy requires high-quality communication and engagement to thrive</a>. Existing political, journalistic and social media systems rarely provide such opportunities, but a growing number of organizations like the center are learning more about how to provide them. </p>

<h2>The story behind the experiment</h2>

<p>Initially, my research centered on national politics. As I learned how issues like <a href="https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Ending-Welfare-as-We-Know-It%3A-President-Clinton-and-Carcasson/d77c809e4e74650afc13886071142497ea89430e">poverty</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1353/rap.2010.0040">race</a> and the <a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1u3AJNv_3HsIZuTiTG4b5yngL7ZHpjMHN/view?usp=sharing">environment</a> were discussed, I became frustrated.</p>

<p>I came to understand that social issues are best understood as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01405730">“wicked problems</a>” that involve competing underlying values that are inherently in <a href="https://cpd.colostate.edu/what-is-deliberation/wicked-problems/">tension with each other</a>. These tensions stand in the way of “solving” the problem long term. In a diverse society where people reasonably prioritize values differently, it is clear that addressing wicked problems requires <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7j_cLqWyunU">a more collaborative style of communication</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754152/original/file-20260814-50-vvqhzj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A narrow security camera mounted to a wall points at black lettering that says What Are You Looking At?" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754152/original/file-20260814-50-vvqhzj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754152/original/file-20260814-50-vvqhzj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754152/original/file-20260814-50-vvqhzj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754152/original/file-20260814-50-vvqhzj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754152/original/file-20260814-50-vvqhzj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754152/original/file-20260814-50-vvqhzj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754152/original/file-20260814-50-vvqhzj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The installment of security cameras exemplifies a wicked problem because there is a clear tension between the underlying values of privacy and security. Issues like this need deeper reflection.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/banksy-royalty-free-image/986384160?adppopup=true">Norbert Bordas/500px via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Research in social psychology and brain science, however, shows humans are simply not wired for these conversations. </p>

<p>Scholarship reveals that humans are <a href="https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/motivated-reasoning">motivated reasoners</a> susceptible to numerous unconscious biases that undermine their ability to engage complex issues. Humans are prone to <a href="https://theconversation.com/cognitive-biases-and-brain-biology-help-explain-why-facts-dont-change-minds-186530">confirmation bias</a> and <a href="https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262045759/the-bias-that-divides-us/">my-side bias</a>, so we tend to cherry-pick the facts that support our preconceived ideas and reject those that challenge them. We often suffer from <a href="https://www.ipgbook.com/the-certainty-trap-products-9781634312561.php">an inflated sense of certainty</a>. </p>

<p>Humans are also narrative creatures who prefer <a href="https://www.jonathangottschall.com/the-story-paradox">simple stories</a> with clear heroes, victims and villains. We have a natural attraction to divisive, <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/U/bo27527354.html">identity-based appeals</a> that too often see the world through us-them frames that lead to <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2019/03/02/opinion/sunday/political-polarization.html">divisiveness and contempt</a>.</p>

<p>In other words, when given a choice, humans strongly prefer to assume that problems are caused by wicked people, rather that engage the inherent wickedness of problems.</p>

<p>By the end of graduate school, I understood that a highly partisan two-party system makes a problematic situation worse by rewarding the exploitation of these human tendencies. As a result, adversarial politics lead to <a href="https://perceptiongap.us/">an exaggerated sense of polarization</a> that breeds divisiveness and misunderstanding. They can also fuel <a href="https://www.upriverpress.com/home/overcoming-information-chaos">information chaos</a>, an overwhelming swirl of misinformation and disinformation that the researchers with RAND aptly named <a href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR2314.html">Truth Decay</a>. Information chaos is also directly related to the erosion of trust in <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/books/the-constitution-of-knowledge/">journalism and academia</a>, two institutions that traditionally helped elevate quality information. </p>

<p>This adversarial environment is also a ripe breeding ground for <a href="https://www.beyondintractability.org/bi24/bad-faith-actors">bad faith actors</a> who undermine our civic culture.  There is a growing recognition among civic engagement scholars and practitioners that <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/democratic-theory/article/conflict-profiteers-are-wrong-revealing-common-ground-the-conditions-for-dialogue-and-the-opportunities-ahead-for-bridging-differences-between-citizens/FD6495C5E251DA00E927263C2095703F">conflict profiteers</a>, <a href="https://www.merchantsofdoubt.org/">merchants of doubt</a> and <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/P/bo24660595.html">polarizers</a> actively work to take advantage of human biases for their own benefit.</p>

<p>Above all, I recognized that <a href="http://www.doi.org/10.1002/ncr.21353">how people engage each other matters</a>. I decided to explore alternative models of engagement better suited to how our brains worked as well as the problems our communities were facing.</p>

<h2>Experimenting in the classroom</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://delibdemjournal.org/">practice of deliberation</a> is a form of structured interactive communication designed to help people engage with complex issues and come to more reasoned judgments. I began experimenting with this new tool in my classroom starting in around 2000. At first I adopted material from the <a href="http://www.nifi.org">National Issues Forums Institute</a>, a nonpartisan organization that has been developing deliberative discussion guides for educational purposes since 1981.</p>

<p>I was hired at Colorado State University in 2003 to take over the argumentation and debate class, and I shifted the class’s focus from debate to deliberation. </p>

<p>The course challenged students to <a href="http://www.communicationcache.com/uploads/1/0/8/8/10887248/reframing_framing.pdf">frame an issue</a> from a deliberative perspective by asking, “What should we do about X?” with X being a shared wicked problem, such as the increasing number of mental health issues on campus. </p>

<p>The assignment shifted students from being advocates of a particular viewpoint to serving as impartial analysts. Many assignments in K-12 and college education ask students to start with a conclusion and then do research to support it,  encouraging motivated reasoning. This assignment was designed to force their brains to see different sides of an issue by adopting what author <a href="https://juliagalef.com/">Julia Galef</a> describes as a “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3MYEtQ5Zdn8">scout mindset</a>.” </p>

<p>Students developed a well-researched discussion guide that outlined at least three distinct approaches to address their problem. These guides served as useful tools for others to overcome my-side bias and exaggerated polarization and to be more likely to, as psychologist Adam Grant has encouraged, <a href="https://adamgrant.net/book/think-again/">think again</a>. </p>

<h2>Taking the conversations outside the classroom</h2>

<p>In 2006, the Center for Public Deliberation launched. </p>

<p>To support it, I designed a  course that trains students to facilitate small-group discussions. Our first major project involved running six nights of forums for the local school district that engaged over 600 participants in a discussion about reorganizing schools. My students and I worked with them to  and successfully debuted a deliberative form of engagement.</p>

<p>Soon we were designing and running events for the city, county, university and community organizations on issues such as housing affordability and decarbonization. College students facilitated every event.</p>

<p>Our work shows that the events our student facilitators supported had a positive impact on the quality of local engagement. Well-designed and well-facilitated processes bring out the best of human nature, particularly our <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/299687/where-good-ideas-come-from-by-steven-johnson/">creativity</a>, <a href="https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250821751/thesocialinstinct/">cooperative social instincts</a> and <a href="https://www.danpink.com/books/drive/">sense of purpose</a>. They can <a href="https://ajph.aphapublications.org/doi/full/10.2105/AJPH.2024.307998">rebuild trust</a> and provide <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/hope-for-democracy-9780190084523">hope for democracy</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/QE2gnUHON80?wmode=transparent&amp;start=3" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Martin Carcasson explains how switching from a focus on positions to a focus on interests can combat wicked problems.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Building local civic capacity nationwide</h2>

<p>Since 2006, <a href="https://cpd.colostate.edu/about-us/staff/">our staff</a> has grown. The center has continued to refine our methods, drawing from the interdisciplinary academic field of <a href="https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/28086">deliberative democracy</a> and using resources from practitioner organizations focused on quality engagement and collaboration, such as the <a href="https://www.ncdd.org/uploads/1/3/5/5/135559674/ncdd2010_resource_guide.pdf">National Coalition for Dialogue and Deliberation</a>, the <a href="https://www.collaborativediscussionproject.com/items">Interactivity Foundation</a> and the <a href="https://www.iap2.org/">International Association for Public Participation</a>. </p>

<p>Similar <a href="https://source.colostate.edu/center-public-deliberation-hosts-kettering-learning-exchange-07062015/">centers for civic life</a> have developed on other campuses. The Center for Public Deliberation is currently a part of a <a href="https://www.jmu.edu/civic/programs/better-conversations-together/centers_for_civic_life_and_faculty_fellows.shtml">Department of Education grant</a> to further expand the network to 40 campuses across the country.</p>

<p>Beyond campus, organizations such as <a href="https://braverangels.org/citizen-led-solutions/">Braver Angels</a>, <a href="https://www.bettertogetheramerica.org/">Better Together America</a> and the <a href="https://trustforciviclife.org/">Trust for Civic Life</a> are dedicated to building local <a href="https://trustforciviclife.org/what-is-a-civic-hub/">civic hubs</a> that use these tools. They also train facilitators and serve as critical <a href="https://www.nationalcivicleague.org/ncr-article/building-community-capacity-in-toxic-times-the-critical-role-of-bridging-institutions/">bridging institutions</a> between diverse groups.</p>

<p>The challenges our communities face are significant. But every day more people are realizing that how we engage each other matters and are making space for the conversations that must be sparked for democracy to thrive. </p>

<p><em>Read more of our stories about <a href="https://theconversation.com/us/boulder-colorado-news">Colorado</a>.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/288679/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Martin Carcasson works for the Colorado State University Center for Public Deliberation, serves as the co-chair of the Braver Angels Civic Scholars Council, and partners with organizations such at National Issues Forum, the Interactivty Foundation, and the National Coalition for Dialogue and Deliberation. </span></em></p></content>

<title>Data center projects in Pennsylvania face stronger local scrutiny after Shapiro’s executive order</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756986/original/file-20260831-60-dk8reu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5000%2C3333&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The cooling towers of an electric station are seen beyond an Amazon Web Services data center construction project in Berwick, Pa.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/the-cooling-towers-of-talen-energys-susquehanna-steam-news-photo/2283985839">Paul Weaver/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Governors across the country are relying on their executive powers to address the increasing <a href="https://www.bostonreview.net/articles/the-ai-data-center-backlash/">public backlash against</a> data center proposals.  </p>

<p>In July 2026, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul placed an <a href="https://www.governor.ny.gov/executive-order/no-62-establishing-temporary-moratorium-data-centers-new-york-while-state-develops">effective moratorium</a> on data center permitting until the state’s Department of Public Service creates a generic environmental impact statement regarding the impacts of data centers. Similarly, in August 2026, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott announced a <a href="https://gov.texas.gov/news/post/governor-abbott-directs-comprehensive-data-center-audit">moratorium on data centers</a> until state agencies can audit data related to impacts on the electric grid. </p>

<p>In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro signed <a href="https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/governor/documents/eo2026_05_protecting%20pennsylvania%20consumers%20from%20data%20center%20impacts_final_executed.pdf">executive order 2026-05</a> on Aug. 18, 2026, placing restrictions on the state’s review of permits related to data centers.  </p>

<p><a href="https://dickinsonlaw.psu.edu/directory/michael-helbing">I am the executive director</a> of Penn State’s <a href="https://celp.psu.edu/about-us/">Center for Energy Law and Policy</a>, and I have been tracking policy responses to data center proposals in Pennsylvania and across the country. I find it notable that one of the justifications the governor appears to cite in his order is a little-used but potentially powerful legal tool: the <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/LI/CT/HTM/00/00.001.027.000..HTM">Environmental Rights Amendment to the Pennsylvania Constitution</a>.</p>



<h2>What the executive order does</h2>

<p>Shapiro’s executive order does not completely stop data center permitting activities. But it does add requirements that may slow their development and give local officials more influence over the process:</p>

<ul>
<li><p>The order makes all data center projects ineligible for the <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/oto/fasttrack">PA Permit Fast Track Program</a>, which streamlines permitting for certain high-impact projects. </p></li>
<li><p>It prohibits any agencies under the governor’s oversight from entering into nondisclosure agreements in connection with a data center project. </p></li>
<li><p>It requires the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection to create a <a href="https://gis.dep.pa.gov/DataCenterPermitTracker/">public map</a> that shows permitting information about all known data center projects in the state.</p></li>
<li><p>Perhaps most significantly, it prohibits officials from issuing state permits for data center projects until after the developer has demonstrated it has complied with local plans and received all required municipal approvals. This ordering of permitting has the potential to enhance local power over data center projects. </p></li>
</ul>

<p>The order also creates a two-tiered system for permitting review. One tier is for developers that agree to comply with the <a href="https://dced.pa.gov/business-assistance/data-center-resources/grid-requirements/">Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development, or GRID, standards</a>. The other is for developers that do not comply. </p>

<p>Among other things, the GRID standards call for developers to secure all energy needed to power their facility, including a portion powered by clean energy; pay 100% of the costs of their project; and comply with environmental operating and reporting requirements.</p>

<p>Developers that agree to comply with the GRID standards will have their state permit applications reviewed on a rolling basis when they are submitted and issued on a rolling basis after all local requirements are met.  </p>

<p>For projects that do not comply with the GRID standards, the state’s Department of Environmental Protection will not even begin reviewing state permit applications until the developers have obtained all necessary local permits.</p>

<p>Collectively, the policies in the executive order are likely to both slow down the permitting process for data centers and give local officials more leverage over data center projects. Municipal officials have <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-pennsylvania-towns-are-protecting-themselves-from-the-noise-heat-and-utility-costs-of-massive-data-centers-282126">significant authority</a> over local land use decisions. Now that state permit review is contingent on local approvals, data center developers will have more incentive to work with local decision-makers to minimize delays.</p>



<h2>The Environmental Rights Amendment</h2>

<p>Beyond the scope of the order itself, I find it significant that the executive order cites “Pennsylvanians’ constitutional rights” as part of its justification. </p>

<p>Although the order does not specify which constitutional rights it is referring to, it appears to be a reference to the <a href="https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&amp;ttl=00&amp;div=0&amp;chapter=1&amp;section=27&amp;subsctn=0">Pennsylvania Constitution’s Environmental Rights Amendment</a>. </p>

<p>The Environmental Rights Amendment is in <a href="https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/LI/CT/HTM/00/00.htm">Article 1 of the Pennsylvania Constitution</a>, along with political rights such as the freedom of speech and freedom of religion. It guarantees the people’s “right to clean air, pure water, and to the preservation of the natural, scenic, historic and esthetic values of the environment.” </p>

<p>Although it was added to the <a href="https://widenerenvironment.com/environmental-law/art-1-sec-27-resources/">state Constitution in 1971</a>, the impact of the Environmental Rights Amendment has been muted until recently. Earlier court decisions limited the legal power of the amendment. But recent opinions from the Pennsylvania Supreme Court have <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3777547">given it new life</a>, raising legal questions about how the amendment will be interpreted in the future. Those cases clarified that it is not necessarily enough for the state to simply comply with environmental statutes. A law or state action that “<a href="https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/pa-supreme-court/1865162.html">unreasonably impairs</a>” the right to clean air, pure water or other environmental values can be deemed unconstitutional.</p>

<p>If the commonwealth cites the Environmental Rights Amendment in litigation defending the executive order on data centers, courts will have another opportunity to interpret the amendment’s language – and therefore its power. Judges will be called upon to weigh how Pennsylvania’s constitutional obligations to protect its citzens’ rights to a clean environment are properly balanced against industry’s procedural and property rights to develop land. Depending on how courts decide those cases, the commonwealth – and even citizens – may have a more robust weapon in their fight for “clean air, pure water, and to the preservation of the natural, scenic, historic and esthetic values of the environment” going forward.</p>

Kathy Hochul placed an effective moratorium on data center permitting until the state’s Department of Public Service creates a generic environmental impact statement regarding the impacts of data centers
Greg Abbott announced a moratorium on data centers until state agencies can audit data related to impacts on the electric grid
Josh Shapiro signed executive order 2026-05 on Aug. 18, 2026, placing restrictions on the state’s review of permits related to data centers
I am the executive director of Penn State’s Center for Energy Law and Policy , and I have been tracking policy responses to data center proposals in Pennsylvania and across the country

This ordering of permitting has the potential to enhance local power over data center projects
The order also creates a two-tiered system for permitting review
One tier is for developers that agree to comply with the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development, or GRID, standards
The other is for developers that do not comply

url:
<title>The greenest building is the one still standing after a disaster</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755772/original/file-20260824-50-qnvssj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=489%2C0%2C3345%2C2230&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption"> Construction choices are often the difference between a house surviving a hurricane or being torn apart.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/homes-and-businesses-along-us-98-are-left-in-devastation-by-news-photo/1051982264?adppopup=true">Mark Wallheiser/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>When Hurricane Michael tore through the Florida Panhandle in 2018, a beach house called the <a href="https://icfmag.com/2019/09/mexico-beach-survivor/">Sand Palace was left standing</a>, while more than half the buildings around it were destroyed. </p>

<p>Its owners had built it to withstand roughly double the wind speed that Florida’s code required, with reinforced concrete walls on 40-foot (12-meter) pilings. The cost was about <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2018/10/15/us/mexico-beach-house-hurricane-trnd">15% to 20% more than standard construction</a>, but the owners wanted a house that could survive storms.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/N7nfH5kNDdg?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The owners of the Sand Palace talk with WJXT4 about why they built the home to survive hurricanes.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Designers usually measure how “green” a building is by its carbon footprint – the greenhouse gases released making, transporting and running everything that goes into it. The Sand Palace’s <a href="https://icfmag.com/2019/09/mexico-beach-survivor/">extra concrete</a> expanded its carbon footprint, making the house appear less environmentally friendly on paper.</p>

<p>But a green building has to last for its intentionally small carbon footprint to make a positive difference. Damage from a flood, a wildfire or a hurricane can require significantly more building materials to repair it, <a href="http://doi.org/10.1007/s44498-026-00152-7">ballooning its carbon footprint over time</a>.</p>

<p>As storms happen more often and with more intensity, considering the full life cycle of a building and its costs over time <a href="https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-17-3">becomes increasingly important</a> to get an accurate picture of how sustainable that building really is.</p>

<h2>Insurance is leading the push for sustainability</h2>

<p>Insurers may be the biggest force <a href="https://www.law.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/archive/2018/06/Stephen-Bushnell-Insurance-Risk-and-Green-Buldings.pdf">getting builders to consider durability</a>.</p>

<p>Building codes are only beginning to take climate change into account. And <a href="https://www.usgbc.org/leed">green ratings like LEED</a> – which encourage builders to make sustainable choices in exchange for the cache of the rating, which can increase property value – assess new buildings when they’re built, not after they’ve been battered by storms.</p>

<p>Insurers, however, have more incentive to <a href="https://www.constructiondive.com/news/building-codes-climate-resilience-nibs/693672/">look at the long-term costs</a>. They <a href="https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/southcentral/2026/03/10/861210.htm">often offer discounts</a> of 15% to 30% off hurricane coverage for fortifying homes because they price a building’s risk over the life of a policy instead of just its condition on Day 1. For builders, that can mean building or retrofitting with reinforced roofing, impact-resistant windows and similar upgrades that meet independently verified wind standards.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755770/original/file-20260824-70-oya4le.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man stands at a railing after a hurricane, looking out at a sea of scattered wood and debris that was once part of buildings. A few houses on stilts are still standing in the background." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755770/original/file-20260824-70-oya4le.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755770/original/file-20260824-70-oya4le.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755770/original/file-20260824-70-oya4le.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755770/original/file-20260824-70-oya4le.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755770/original/file-20260824-70-oya4le.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755770/original/file-20260824-70-oya4le.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755770/original/file-20260824-70-oya4le.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Hurricane Helene left a mess when it made landfall in Horseshoe Beach, Fla., on Sept. 28, 2024. Some homes fared better than others.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/david-hester-inspects-damages-of-his-house-after-hurricane-news-photo/2174219458?adppopup=true">Chandan Khanna/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Studies that measure how much damage could be avoided from resilient design have found a similar payoff.</p>

<p>For example, a study of flood-prevention infrastructure in coastal Catalonia, Spain, found that flood barriers and channel improvements generated more greenhouse gas emissions during construction, but they <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2016.12.034">prevented an estimated 58 metric tons of carbon-equivalent emissions</a> per flood. Within 25 years, the emissions avoided from damage were expected to balance out the emissions from the improvements, well inside the infrastructure’s 50-year expected lifespan. Financially, the payback was far faster: about two years.</p>

<h2>Getting resilience into the calculation</h2>

<p>The next step is expanding that logic into standards that already shape most construction decisions.</p>

<p>Researchers, including myself, are proposing <a href="http://doi.org/10.1007/s44498-026-00152-7">ways to bring resilience into the equation</a>. Accounting for the materials, energy and disruption to a building during and after a disaster would show the true costs of a building that’s too damaged to function.</p>





<p>Three pieces are missing from that equation right now:</p>

<p>The first is the cost of keeping people and operations running while a damaged building is out of commission: temporary shelter, emergency generators, transportation for evacuated residents or relocated staff. None of that currently <a href="http://doi.org/10.1007/s44498-026-00152-7">counts toward a building’s environmental footprint</a> even though it’s a direct consequence of how that building was designed.</p>

<p>The second is the cost of adapting a building after an event – not just repairing it, but upgrading it to withstand the next one. That might include reinforcing a foundation that failed, elevating utilities that flooded, or replacing what was there with something built to survive next time. Each <a href="http://doi.org/10.1007/s44498-026-00152-7">carries environmental costs</a> that current assessments don’t measure. </p>

<p>The third is recognizing the damage, repairs and downtime that a resilient design choice helps a building’s owners and tenants avoid altogether. Examples already exist, like the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2016.12.034">coastal infrastructure case in Spain</a>. What’s missing is automatically including these benefits into green-building and infrastructure assessments.</p>

<p>Together, <a href="http://doi.org/10.1007/s44498-026-00152-7">these show up as real costs</a> – in dollars, in carbon emissions and in the lives disrupted when a hospital or home loses functionality for months instead of days. They’re costs that insurers, the designers of building codes and ratings systems all have a reason to shrink.</p>

<p>We already know how to build homes like the Sand Palace that can stand up to disasters. What’s missing isn’t the engineering; it’s incentive to build for durability as the rule rather than the exception.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290313/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
